voice_text: This video explains the revised proposal for Aadi Project Tracker. The business now wants to answer one question: what does each project cost us in people, what is that effort worth, and are we making money, by employee, by project and by project tag. The screens you see are the interactive prototype, built from your Excel workbook. All names and salaries in it are fictional stand ins, with the same percentages and arithmetic as the workbook.

First, the employee master. Each employee has one department, a title and a monthly salary. Every department has a Head of Department, which can be changed here and is audited. Salary is a restricted field. Only the owner and finance see it, and the server hides it from everyone else. The list also shows who is fully allocated and who is on the bench.
Adding an employee is validated. A name and a salary above zero are required, and a department must be chosen. Nothing is saved in this prototype.

Next, the project master with tags. Tags are a managed list, and a project can carry several. Here we filter by Marketing, then also by Customer. The numbers above the table follow the filter, so any financial view can be sliced by tag. We can also add a new tag, and tag names must be unique.

Now allocation. Each cell is the percentage of an employee's month spent on a project, and one person can work on many projects. The total per person can never exceed one hundred percent. If we try to give Esha fifty percent on the first project, when she is already at one hundred, the entry is rejected with a clear message. Giving Ananya, who is on the bench, fifty percent on the third project works, and her free capacity drops to fifty percent.
Reset brings back the baseline from the workbook: fourteen employees, eleven projects, and three people on the bench.

Settings hold the two numbers from your guidelines: one hundred sixty working hours a month and an hourly rate of two hundred fifty rupees. They are organization defaults. We propose that the rate can be overridden for a project and the hours for a part time employee. Watch the totals on the right when the rate changes to three hundred, and when one project gets its own rate of four hundred.

Effort and cost. Effort is allocation times monthly hours. Cost is allocation times the employee's own monthly salary. Opening Chitra Pillai shows the steps: fifty percent on two projects, eighty hours each, and ten thousand rupees each. Bench hours and bench cost show capacity that is paid for but not allocated.

By project, the first project is the worked example. Four people give four hundred hours, worth one lakh rupees at the standard rate. The salary cost is fifty two thousand five hundred rupees, so the margin is forty seven thousand five hundred.
And by tag. A project with two tags appears under both, so tag rows overlap and are not meant to be added together. The tag analysis screen offers an additive view as well.

Revenue targets are set per project and per month. In your workbook only three projects have a target. The others show a warning, not a misleading zero. We set a target of ninety thousand rupees on the Aadi Product Suite and immediately see how planned value compares with the target and with cost.

Project profitability. Margin is the revenue basis minus salary cost. With the standard value basis, the organization earns two lakh forty thousand rupees on allocated work, a margin of fifty four point five percent. The unallocated salary of sixty thousand rupees is shown on its own line, so the bench is never hidden. Switching to the target basis only includes projects that have a target.

The categories from your targets sheet, such as infrastructure, third party, marketing and sales, can be added as an optional layer. It is off by default, because whether they belong in profitability is a decision for you.

Tag wise analysis shows hours, value, cost and margin per tag, with a drill down to the projects. Opening the Marketing tag lists its projects. With primary tag only, every project is counted once, and the rows add up to the organization total.

This screen compares your workbook with the corrected calculation. Hours and value agree. The cost does not. On projects two to eleven the workbook multiplies every allocation by one fixed salary cell of thirty thousand rupees, instead of each person's own salary. It reports three lakh seven thousand five hundred rupees. The correct cost is two lakh rupees. We need you to confirm this correction.

Roles matter. Switching to Operations, the effort screen still works in hours, but salary, cost and value are restricted. A project manager sees only assigned projects, and no salary data. The platform administrator sees none of it. These limits are enforced by the server in the real product.

To finish, the proposal lists the decisions we need from you. The main ones are what counts as revenue, whether the corrected cost is right, whether cost is planned or from actual timesheets, what the S and H markers mean, whether non salary costs are included, and how tags and heads of department should work. Each has a recommended answer. The product requirements document, the handoff notes for Cursor, and this prototype are ready for your review. No production code has been changed.
